sentences.text: Iracema lived in Manaus, the big city in the middle of the Amazon.
She was ten.
But every year in July, for four weeks, she took the small passenger boat two days up the Rio Negro to a very small village called São João da Mata, where her grandmother lived.
São João da Mata was a ribeirinho community — one of the small settlements of river-people scattered along the banks of the great rivers of the Amazon.
There were maybe eighty people in it.

It had one small school, one small church, one small general store, and about twenty houses, all built up on tall wooden stilts because the river rose and fell many meters between the wet and dry seasons.
Iracema's grandmother, Vovó Marisel, was seventy-six.
She was small and thin and had straight white hair that she wore in a single long braid down her back.
She had lived in São João da Mata her whole life.
Her mother had lived there before her.
And her mother's mother, and so on, back many generations.
The family was mixed — mostly of caboclo people, which meant a mix of indigenous and Portuguese ancestry, going back centuries.
Vovó Marisel spoke Portuguese but also spoke Nheengatu, an old lingua franca that had been used in the Amazon for hundreds of years and that almost nobody spoke anymore.
She was one of maybe six people in the village who still knew it well.
Vovó's house was small — one main room with a wood stove at one end, a small back room with a proper bed for guests, and a wide wooden porch at the front that looked out over the river.
Vovó slept in a hammock in the main room.
Iracema slept in the bed.
There was no electricity in the house.
There was a small solar panel that ran a single light bulb and could charge a phone.
There was no running water — you carried water up from the river in a bucket, and boiled it before you drank it.
Iracema loved being at Vovó's.
She loved the sounds — the river lapping under the house at high water, the frogs at night, the parrots at dawn, the wet howl of the howler monkeys deep in the forest sometimes.
She loved the food — river fish, cassava flour, small papayas from the tree behind the house.
She loved being with Vovó, who talked slowly and never seemed to be in a hurry.
Manaus, which was where Iracema lived the rest of the year with her mother and stepfather, was fast and loud.
São João da Mata was slow and quiet.
Both were true.
Iracema needed both.
On the third evening of Iracema's visit, Vovó Marisel called her out onto the porch.
It was about seven o'clock.
The sun had set.
The sky over the river was purple and gold.
Vovó sat down on the wooden bench that ran along the porch railing.
She patted the bench beside her.
Iracema sat down.
Vovó was quiet for a long moment.
Then she said, "Iracema.
This year I want to take you to a small ceremony.
It happens once a year, in July.
Very few people go.
Just — three or four of us.
This year I want you to come.
If you want." Iracema said, "What kind of ceremony."
"It is very small," said Vovó.
"It is not a religious ceremony — not exactly.
It is an old thing.
From before the church.
It has been in our family — the women in our family — for maybe two hundred years.
Maybe more.
My mother taught me.
Her mother taught her.
It is called a nomeação de rio — a river-naming.
On a specific night in July, when the moon is a specific shape, three women go out in a canoe onto the river, at a specific bend.
And we — we speak the names of our dead into the river.
That is all.
We say the names out loud.
The river hears them.
Then we go home."
Iracema said, "What does that do.
What is it for." Vovó Marisel thought for a while.
She said, "That is the question I asked my mother when she first told me about it.
She said — it is for the dead.
And it is for us.
She said that when a person dies, their name is one of the things that survives them longest.
If nobody says their name, eventually the name is gone.
And when the name is gone, the person is really gone.
So we — the women in our family — we go to the river once a year and we say the names.
All the names.
Our dead.
Our mothers' dead.
Their mothers' dead.
Going back many generations.
We say them out loud so the river hears.
And the river carries them.
That is what she told me."
"Does the river really — hear," Iracema said.
Vovó Marisel smiled a small smile.
She said, "I do not know if the river hears the way you and I hear.
I am not sure.
But I know that when we say the names, the names — feel spoken.
That is a real thing.
Whether the river is doing anything or not, we are doing something.
We are keeping the names alive.
That is what my mother said.
That is what her mother said.
Do you want to come this year."
Iracema said, "Yes.
I want to come." Vovó said, "Good.
It is on Saturday night.
Four days from now.
Between now and then I want you to help me remember the names.
I do it every year — it is a long list, going back hundreds of years, and it is easy to forget one.
My mother made me memorize them.
I will teach you the ones from our family.
You do not have to memorize them all this year.
You just have to know them well enough to help me say them.
Yes?" Iracema nodded.
"There is one more thing," said Vovó.
"Every woman who goes on the canoe adds — at the end — the names of her own most recent dead.
Not the ones from the long list.
The recent ones.
The ones we knew ourselves.
I add the names of my mother and my father, and my sister who died in the flu three years ago, and my husband.
This year — if you come — you should think about what names you want to add.
From your own life.
You must have some."
